title: German grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is everyday Standard German as people speak it in Germany.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first German conversation.
lessons.topic: {{ich bin}}, {{ich heiße}}, {{ich komme aus}}; the two words for “you”: {{du}} and {{Sie}}

goal.t: Hallo, ich heiße Anna. Ich komme aus Kanada.
goal.tr: Hello, my name is Anna. I'm from Canada.

dialog.t: Hallo! Ich bin Jonas.
dialog.tr: Hi! I'm Jonas.

dialog.t: Hallo, ich heiße Anna.
dialog.tr: Hi, my name is Anna.

dialog.t: Woher kommst du?
dialog.tr: Where are you from?

dialog.t: Ich komme aus Kanada. Und du?
dialog.tr: I'm from Canada. And you?

dialog.t: Ich komme aus Hamburg.
dialog.tr: I'm from Hamburg.

dialog.t: Freut mich!
dialog.tr: Nice to meet you!

blocks.p: Three ways to say who you are, all usable today: {{Ich bin Jonas.}} “I'm Jonas.”, {{Ich heiße Anna.}} “My name is Anna.” (word for word “I am called Anna”), and {{Ich komme aus Kanada.}} “I come from Canada.”

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Canada.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, she, it.
a word for an action or a state: come, live, be, want.

blocks.p: **I.** {{ich}} is “I”. Unlike English “I”, it has no capital letter, except at the start of a sentence. When you talk about yourself, most verbs end in {{-e}}: {{ich heiße}}, {{ich komme}}, {{ich wohne}} “I live”. {{ich bin}} “I am” is the odd one out.

**You: du or Sie.** German has two words for “you”. {{du}} is for friends, family, children, and people your age in a relaxed setting. {{Sie}} (always with a capital S) is for strangers, shop staff, your boss: anyone you'd call Mr. or Ms. The verb changes with them:

ex.note: said by a woman; a man says {{Lehrer}}. With jobs, German leaves out “a”.

ex.t: Guten Tag, ich bin Frau Weber.
ex.note: {{Guten Tag}} is the polite hello during the day
most countries need no “the”: {{aus Kanada}}, {{aus Spanien}}; a few do: {{aus den USA}}, {{aus der Schweiz}}

blocks.tip: {{ß}} is a German letter for a sharp “ss” sound: {{heißen}} sounds like “HY-sen”. And when you're not sure whether to say {{du}} or {{Sie}}, say {{Sie}}: people will offer you {{du}} if they want it.

mistakes.why: {{heiße}} already means “am called”, so there's no room for {{bin}}. Say {{Ich bin Anna}} or {{Ich heiße Anna}}.
With {{du}}, the verb ends in {{-st}}. {{-en}} is for {{Sie}}.
For your job, German says just the job, with no word for “a”.

practice.q: You're talking to a hotel receptionist you've never met. “You” is…
practice.why: A stranger at work: {{Sie}}. {{du}} is for friends, family and children.

practice.tr: I'm from Canada.
practice.why: With {{ich}}, the verb ends in {{-e}}: {{ich komme}}.

practice.q: You're Tom, from London. Choose your replies.

lines.why: About yourself: {{ich}}. {{du heißt}} would be “your name is”.

practice.tr: What's your name? (polite)

practice.q: Ask a friend: “Where are you from?”
Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{Hallo, ich heiße…}}

answers.tr: Hello, my name is Sarah. I'm from England.

answers.tr: Hi, I'm David. I'm from Canada and I live in Munich.

lessons.title: Ask someone about themselves
lessons.summary: Ask where someone lives, what they do and which languages they speak, and understand the answers.
lessons.topic: Question words ({{wer, was, wo, woher, wie}}); verb endings {{-e}}, {{-st}}, {{-en}}; the verb in second place

goal.t: Wo wohnst du und was machst du beruflich?
goal.tr: Where do you live and what do you do for a living?

dialog.t: Wie heißt du?
dialog.tr: What's your name?

dialog.t: Ich heiße Ben. Und du?
dialog.tr: I'm Ben. And you?

dialog.t: Mia. Wo wohnst du, Ben?
dialog.tr: Mia. Where do you live, Ben?

dialog.t: Ich wohne in Köln. Und du?
dialog.tr: I live in Cologne. And you?

blocks.means: a word that asks for information: who, what, where, how.

table: {{Was machst du?}} What are you doing?
{{Wo wohnst du?}} Where do you live?
{{Woher kommst du?}} Where are you from?

blocks.p: **The verb comes second.** This is the most important rule of German word order: in a sentence that tells or asks for information, the verb is the **second** thing. In a question, the question word is first and the verb comes right after it: {{Wo wohnst du?}}, word for word “Where live you?”. English needs “do” (“Where *do* you live?”); German never does: the verb itself moves up.
It's the second *thing*, not always the second word: in {{Mia und ich wohnen in Bonn.}}, “Mia and I” is one thing, and {{wohnen}} comes after it. You'll meet this rule in every lesson.

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: {{wohnen}} “to live”, {{machen}} “to do, to make”. In German it almost always ends in {{-en}}.

blocks.p: **Endings.** To use a verb, take the infinitive, drop {{-en}}, and add the ending for who's doing it: {{-e}} for {{ich}}, {{-st}} for {{du}}, and {{-en}} (the same as the infinitive) for {{Sie}}.

ex.t: Was lernst du? – Ich lerne Deutsch.
ex.tr: What are you learning? – I'm learning German.

ex.note: short for {{Wie geht es dir?}}; to a stranger: {{Wie geht es Ihnen?}}

blocks.tip: If a verb's stem ends in {{-t}} or {{-d}}, an extra {{e}} makes it easy to say: {{du arbeitest}}, {{du findest}}. If it ends in {{-s}}, {{-ß}} or {{-z}}, {{du}} adds only {{-t}}: {{du heißt}}.

mistakes.why: After a question word, the verb comes second: before {{du}}.
{{-en}} is for {{Sie}}; with {{du}}, the verb ends in {{-st}}.

lessons.title: Talk about other people
lessons.summary: Introduce a friend and say where people live and what they do: “This is Lena. She's from Vienna.”
lessons.topic: {{er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie}}; the whole present of regular verbs and of {{sein}} “to be”

goal.t: Das ist Lena. Sie kommt aus Wien und wohnt jetzt in Berlin.
goal.tr: This is Lena. She's from Vienna and lives in Berlin now.

dialog.t: Hallo Paul! Das ist Lena.
dialog.tr: Hi Paul! This is Lena.

dialog.t: Hallo Lena! Woher kommst du?
dialog.tr: Hi Lena! Where are you from?

dialog.t: Ich komme aus Wien.
dialog.tr: I'm from Vienna.

dialog.t: Lena und ich arbeiten zusammen.
dialog.tr: Lena and I work together.

dialog.t: Ah, ihr seid Kolleginnen!
dialog.tr: Oh, you're colleagues!

blocks.p: **Das ist…** “This is…” or “That is…” introduces anyone: {{Das ist Lena.}} {{Das ist Herr Becker.}}
Here is every person a verb can have. The endings follow a pattern, and {{sein}} “to be” is irregular, as “be” is in English:

Two things make it easier than it looks. {{wir}}, {{sie}} “they” and {{Sie}} “you” always share one form, which is the infinitive for every verb except {{sein}}. And {{er/sie/es}} and {{ihr}} both end in {{-t}}.

**sie, sie and Sie.** {{sie}} is “she” and also “they”; {{Sie}} with a capital is the polite “you”. The verb tells you which: {{sie wohnt}} “she lives”, {{sie wohnen}} “they live” (or, with a capital, “you live”).
**ihr** is “you” for two or more people you'd each call {{du}}: friends, family, children. For one stranger or several, it's {{Sie}}.

ex.t: Er heißt Paul und arbeitet in Hamburg.
ex.tr: His name is Paul and he works in Hamburg.

ex.t: Das ist Herr Becker. Er ist Lehrer.
ex.tr: This is Mr. Becker. He's a teacher.

blocks.tip: {{Herr}} is “Mr.” and {{Frau}} “Ms.” or “Mrs.”, with the last name: {{Herr Becker}}, {{Frau Weber}}. Someone you call that, you call {{Sie}}.

mistakes.why: One person (she): {{-t}}. {{-en}} is for we, they and the polite you.
{{sein}} is irregular: with {{ihr}} it's {{seid}}.

options: “They live in Berlin” or “You live in Berlin” (polite)
practice.why: “She lives” is {{sie wohnt}}. With {{wohnen}}, it's “they” or the polite “you”: the situation (and in writing the capital S) tells them apart.

practice.tr: We're from Italy.
practice.why: {{wir sind}} “we are”. {{seid}} goes with {{ihr}}, {{ist}} with one person.

practice.tr: Paul works in Hamburg.
practice.why: One person: {{-t}}, with an extra {{e}} after the {{t}} of {{arbeit-}}.

practice.tr: Lena and I work together.

Guten Tag, Frau Schulz! Das sind Marco.

lessons.title: Ask yes-or-no questions and say no
lessons.summary: Ask “Are you…?” and “Do you…?”, answer yes or no, and say what isn't so.
lessons.topic: The verb first in yes/no questions; {{nicht}} “not”; {{ja}}, {{nein}} and {{doch}}

goal.t: Wohnst du hier? – Nein, ich wohne nicht hier.
goal.tr: Do you live here? – No, I don't live here.

dialog.t: Entschuldigung, ist hier noch frei?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, is this seat free?

dialog.t: Ja, bitte.
dialog.tr: Yes, go ahead.

dialog.t: Danke. Fahren Sie auch nach Köln?
dialog.tr: Thanks. Are you going to Cologne too?

dialog.t: Nein, nach Bonn. Wohnen Sie in Köln?
dialog.tr: No, to Bonn. Do you live in Cologne?

dialog.t: Nein, ich wohne nicht in Köln. Ich besuche dort meine Schwester.
dialog.tr: No, I don't live in Cologne. I'm visiting my sister there.

blocks.p: **The verb first.** For a question you answer with yes or no, put the verb at the very start: {{Du wohnst hier.}} “You live here.” becomes {{Wohnst du hier?}} “Do you live here?” Again, no “do”: the verb itself moves to the front.
So German has two kinds of question. With a question word, the verb is second; without one, the verb is first:

**nicht** “not” comes after the verb, never before it. Put it at the end of the sentence, or before a place ({{nicht hier}}, {{nicht in Köln}}) or a describing word ({{nicht müde}}): {{Ich komme nicht.}} {{Ich wohne nicht hier.}} {{Er ist nicht müde.}}

**ja, nein, doch.** {{ja}} is “yes” and {{nein}} “no”. German has a third answer English doesn't: {{doch}} is “yes” as the answer to a question with “not” in it, when you disagree with it: {{Kommst du nicht? – Doch!}} “Aren't you coming? – Yes, I am!”

ex.t: Kommen Sie aus Österreich? – Nein, aus der Schweiz.
ex.tr: Are you from Austria? – No, from Switzerland.

ex.t: Arbeitet Paul heute? – Nein, heute nicht.
ex.tr: Is Paul working today? – No, not today.

ex.t: Kommst du heute nicht? – Doch, natürlich!
ex.tr: Aren't you coming today? – Yes, of course I am!

blocks.tip: As in English, a statement with a rising voice is also a question: {{Du kommst aus Kanada?}} “You're from Canada?”

mistakes.why: {{nicht}} comes after the verb, never between {{ich}} and the verb.

mistakes.wrong: Kommst du nicht? – Ja, ich komme!
mistakes.right: Kommst du nicht? – Doch, ich komme!
mistakes.tr: Aren't you coming? – Yes, I am!
mistakes.why: To say “yes” against a question with {{nicht}}, use {{doch}}.

practice.q: A friend asks {{Bist du nicht müde?}} “Aren't you tired?” You are tired. You say…
practice.why: You disagree with the “not” in the question, so it's {{doch}}. {{Nein}} would mean “No, I'm not tired.”

practice.tr: Do you live in Berlin?
I don't understand that.
practice.why: “Not” in a sentence is {{nicht}}; {{nein}} is the answer “no”.

practice.tr: Where do you live? – In Cologne.
practice.why: The answer is a place, so the question word is {{wo}}, and the verb comes right after it.

practice.q: On the train: answer the woman next to you.

lines.tr: Excuse me, are you going to Munich?

options: Nein, ich fahre nicht nach München.
Nein, ich nicht fahre nach München.

lines.why: {{Ja}} stands outside the sentence; then comes a normal statement: {{ich}}, then the verb.

lessons.title: Name things around you
lessons.summary: Point at things and name them: “The station is over there.” Every German noun is der, die or das.
lessons.topic: Nouns and their capital letter; {{der, die, das}} “the”; {{er, sie, es}} for “it”

goal.t: Der Bahnhof ist da drüben.
goal.tr: The station is over there.

dialog.t: Entschuldigung, wo ist der Bahnhof?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, where's the station?

dialog.t: Der Bahnhof? Er ist da drüben.
dialog.tr: The station? It's over there.

dialog.t: Und die Post?
dialog.tr: And the post office?

dialog.t: Die Post ist hier gleich links.
dialog.tr: The post office is right here on the left.

dialog.t: Danke! Ist das Hotel Adler weit?
dialog.tr: Thanks! Is the Hotel Adler far?

dialog.t: Nein, es ist nicht weit.
dialog.tr: No, it's not far.

blocks.means: a word for a person, an animal, a thing or an idea: man, dog, station, love.

blocks.p: **Capital letters.** In German, every noun starts with a capital letter, wherever it is in the sentence: {{der Bahnhof}}, {{die Post}}, {{das Hotel}}. That makes them easy to spot.

blocks.means: a little word in front of a noun, like “the” or “a”.
the group a noun belongs to. German nouns are masculine, feminine or neuter, and the group decides which “the” they take.

blocks.p: **der, die, das.** English has one “the”; German has three, one for each gender: {{der}} (masculine), {{die}} (feminine) and {{das}} (neuter). The gender belongs to the word, not to the thing: a table is masculine, a lamp feminine, a book neuter. For people, it usually matches: {{der Mann}} “the man”, {{die Frau}} “the woman”.

**So learn every noun with its der, die or das**, as one word: not just {{Tisch}}, but {{der Tisch}}. A few hints help: nouns ending in {{-e}} are mostly {{die}} ({{die Lampe}}, {{die Straße}}); nouns ending in {{-ung}}, {{-heit}} or {{-keit}} are always {{die}}; nouns ending in {{-chen}} are always {{das}} ({{das Mädchen}} “the girl”).

**“It” is er, sie or es.** For “it”, German uses the pronoun that matches the noun's gender: {{der Bahnhof}} → {{er}}, {{die Post}} → {{sie}}, {{das Hotel}} → {{es}}. So {{Er ist da drüben.}} can mean “It's over there” (the station).

ex.t: Wo ist der Schlüssel? – Er ist hier.
Wie ist die Pizza? – Sie ist super!

blocks.tip: The basics course shows every noun with its {{der}}, {{die}} or {{das}}. Learn them together from the start, and say them aloud together: {{der Tisch, die Tür, das Buch}}.

mistakes.wrong: Der Tisch ist neu. Es ist schön.
mistakes.right: Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist schön.
mistakes.tr: The table is new. It's nice.
mistakes.why: {{der Tisch}} is masculine, so “it” is {{er}}.
Nouns always start with a capital letter.

practice.why: Most nouns ending in {{-e}} are feminine (a few, like {{der Name}}, aren't).

lessons.title: Ask what something is
lessons.summary: Ask “What's that?” and answer “That's a…” or “That's not a…, it's a…”.
lessons.topic: {{ein, eine}} “a”; {{kein, keine}} “not a, no”; {{Was ist das?}}

goal.t: Was ist das? – Das ist kein Hotel, das ist ein Krankenhaus.
goal.tr: What's that? – That's not a hotel, it's a hospital.

dialog.t: Was ist das?
dialog.tr: What's that?

dialog.t: Das ist eine Brezel.
dialog.tr: That's a pretzel.

dialog.t: Und das? Ist das ein Brötchen?
dialog.tr: And that? Is that a roll?

dialog.t: Nein, das ist kein Brötchen. Das ist ein Berliner.
dialog.tr: No, that's not a roll. That's a Berliner, a jelly doughnut.

dialog.t: Lecker!
dialog.tr: Yummy!

blocks.p: **a: ein or eine.** “A” follows gender too, but it has only two forms here: {{ein}} for masculine and neuter nouns, {{eine}} for feminine ones.

**kein** is {{k}} + {{ein}}: “not a” or “no”. German never says {{nicht ein}}: {{Das ist kein Hotel.}} “That's not a hotel.” {{kein}} also says “no, not any” in front of nouns that have no article at all: {{Ich habe keine Zeit.}} “I have no time.”

**nicht or kein?** Use {{kein}} to say no to a noun that would have “a” or nothing in front of it ({{ein Auto}} → {{kein Auto}}; {{Zeit}} → {{keine Zeit}}). Use {{nicht}} for everything else: verbs, describing words, and nouns with “the” ({{Das ist nicht der Bus.}}).
**Das ist…** works for everything. This {{das}} means “this” or “that”, and it never changes with the gender: {{Das ist ein Tisch.}} {{Das ist eine Lampe.}}

ex.t: Was ist das? – Das ist ein Kühlschrank.
Das ist nicht der Bus nach Köln.
ex.tr: That isn't the bus to Cologne.

ex.t: Wer ist das? – Das ist Frau Lange, eine Kollegin.
ex.tr: Who's that? – That's Ms. Lange, a colleague.

blocks.tip: {{Kein Problem!}} “No problem!” is one of the most useful things you can say in German, and it's built just like the lesson.

mistakes.why: “Not a” is {{kein}}, never {{nicht ein}}.
{{die Lampe}} is feminine, so “a” is {{eine}}.

practice.tr: That's no problem.

practice.t: Das ist ___ der Bus nach Köln.
practice.tr: That isn't the bus to Cologne.
practice.why: With {{der}}, it's {{nicht}}: {{kein}} only replaces “a” or no article.

Und das? Ist eine Brezel das?

answers.tr: No, that's not a hotel. It's a school.

answers.t: Nein, das ist kein Hotel, das ist ein Krankenhaus.
answers.tr: No, that's not a hotel, it's a hospital.

lessons.title: Count things and ask the price
lessons.summary: Count to a hundred, say “two coffees” or “three children”, and ask what things cost.
lessons.topic: Plurals (and {{die}} for all of them); numbers; {{Was kostet…?}} and {{Was kosten…?}}

goal.t: Was kosten die Äpfel? – Zwei Euro das Kilo.
goal.tr: How much are the apples? – Two euros a kilo.

dialog.t: Guten Tag! Was kosten die Tomaten?
dialog.tr: Hello! How much are the tomatoes?

dialog.t: Drei Euro das Kilo.
dialog.tr: Three euros a kilo.

dialog.t: Und was kostet die Melone?
dialog.tr: And how much is the melon?

dialog.t: Zwei Euro fünfzig.
dialog.tr: Two fifty.

dialog.t: Gut, ein Kilo Tomaten und zwei Melonen, bitte.
dialog.tr: OK, a kilo of tomatoes and two melons, please.

dialog.t: Das macht acht Euro.
dialog.tr: That's eight euros.

blocks.means: the form of a noun for more than one: house → houses.

blocks.p: **Plurals.** English mostly adds -s. German has a few endings, and some nouns also put two dots on a vowel ({{a}} → {{ä}}, {{o}} → {{ö}}, {{u}} → {{ü}}). The good news: in the plural, “the” is always {{die}}, whatever the gender.
So learn each noun with its plural, as dictionaries give it: {{der Tag, die Tage}}. Feminine nouns are the easiest: almost all of them add {{-n}} or {{-en}}.

**Numbers.** {{eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn}}, then {{elf}} 11 and {{zwölf}} 12, then {{-zehn}}: {{dreizehn}} 13 … {{neunzehn}} 19. The tens end in {{-zig}}: {{zwanzig}} 20, {{dreißig}} 30, {{vierzig}} 40, {{fünfzig}} 50 … {{hundert}} 100. From 21 on, German says the ones first, like the old English “four-and-twenty”: {{einundzwanzig}} 21, {{fünfundvierzig}} 45.

**How much?** {{Was kostet…?}} for one thing, {{Was kosten…?}} for several: the verb follows the noun, like “is” and “are”: {{Was kostet das Brot?}} “How much is the bread?”, {{Was kosten die Brötchen?}} “How much are the rolls?”

ex.note: drinks you order, and measures after a number, stay singular: {{zwei Kaffee}}, {{zwei Kilo}}, {{fünf Euro}}

ex.tr: How much is that? – Fifteen euros.

ex.t: Wie viele Leute kommen? – Ungefähr zwanzig.
ex.tr: How many people are coming? – About twenty.

blocks.tip: {{sechzehn}} 16 and {{sechzig}} 60 drop the {{s}} of {{sechs}}; {{siebzehn}} 17 and {{siebzig}} 70 drop the {{en}} of {{sieben}}. And Germans write prices with a comma: {{2,50 €}}, said {{zwei Euro fünfzig}}.

mistakes.why: More than one: the verb is plural too, {{sind}}.
{{die Äpfel}} is plural, so the verb is {{kosten}}.
The ones come first, then {{und}}, then the tens: {{vier-und-fünfzig}}.

practice.why: One “the” for every plural: {{die Tage}}, {{die Frauen}}, {{die Kinder}}.

lessons.summary: Say what people and things are like: “The apartment is small, but very nice.”
lessons.topic: Adjectives after {{sein}} (no ending); {{sehr, ziemlich, zu}}; {{und, aber, oder}}

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: big, old, nice, expensive.

blocks.p: **After sein, adjectives have no ending.** When an adjective comes after {{sein}} “to be”, it never changes, whatever the gender or number: {{Der Tisch ist neu.}} {{Die Lampe ist neu.}} {{Die Bücher sind neu.}} (In front of a noun it does change, as in {{ein neuer Tisch}}: that's for a later lesson.)

**How much?** {{sehr}} “very”, {{ziemlich}} “quite, pretty”, {{zu}} “too”, {{total}} “really” (casual) and {{nicht so}} “not that”: {{sehr gut}}, {{ziemlich alt}}, {{zu teuer}}, {{nicht so teuer}}. And for “not” with an adjective, it's {{nicht}}: {{Das ist nicht teuer.}}

**und, aber, oder.** {{und}} “and”, {{aber}} “but” and {{oder}} “or” join two sentences without changing either: the verb stays second in both. {{Die Wohnung ist klein, aber sie ist schön.}} Put a comma before {{aber}}.

ex.t: Mein Deutsch ist nicht so gut.
Berlin ist groß und ziemlich laut.
ex.tr: Berlin is big and pretty loud.

blocks.tip: {{schön}} means “beautiful”, but very often just “nice”: {{Schönes Wochenende!}} “Have a nice weekend!” For people, “nice, kind” is {{nett}}.

mistakes.why: After {{sein}}, an adjective has no ending.
{{kein}} goes with nouns. With an adjective, “not” is {{nicht}}.

practice.why: After {{sein}}, no ending, even in the plural.

practice.tr: The coffee is too hot!

lessons.title: Say what you have
lessons.summary: Say what you have and don't have (a brother, a dog, time) and meet the accusative: the form for what you have, want, buy and see.
lessons.topic: {{haben}}; the accusative: {{den}}, {{einen}}, {{keinen}} (only masculine nouns change)

goal.t: Ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester.
goal.tr: I have a brother and a sister.

dialog.t: Hast du Geschwister?
dialog.tr: Do you have brothers and sisters?

dialog.t: Ja, ich habe einen Bruder. Und du?
dialog.tr: Yes, I have a brother. And you?

dialog.t: Ich habe keine Geschwister, aber ich habe einen Hund!
dialog.tr: I don't have any brothers or sisters, but I have a dog!

dialog.t: Oh, wie heißt er?
dialog.tr: Oh, what's his name?

dialog.t: Bello. Hast du auch ein Haustier?
dialog.tr: Bello. Do you have a pet too?

dialog.t: Nein, ich habe kein Haustier.
dialog.tr: No, I don't have a pet.

blocks.means: the person or thing that does the action, or that is something: **I** have a dog; **the bus** is late.
the person or thing the action is done to: I have **a dog**; I see **the bus**.
the form German uses for the object of most verbs: what you have, want, buy, see, eat or need.

blocks.p: **Subject and object.** In {{Ich habe einen Hund.}}, {{ich}} is the subject and {{einen Hund}} the object. German shows the object by changing the article in front of it, and you'll need that all the time: for what you have, want, buy, see, need, eat and drink.
**Only masculine nouns change**, so it's less work than it sounds: {{der}} → {{den}}, {{ein}} → {{einen}}, {{kein}} → {{keinen}}. Feminine, neuter and plural nouns stay exactly as they are.

ex.t: Wir haben ein Auto, aber keinen Garten.
ex.tr: We have a car, but no yard.

ex.note: word for word “I have no hunger”

blocks.tip: Germans “have” some feelings that English speakers “are”: {{Ich habe Hunger.}} “I'm hungry.”, {{Ich habe Durst.}} “I'm thirsty.”, {{Ich habe Angst.}} “I'm scared.” And “not” is {{kein}}: {{Ich habe keine Angst.}}

mistakes.why: {{der Bruder}} is masculine, and it's the object (what you have): {{einen}}.
{{haben}} is a little irregular: {{du hast}}, {{er hat}}.
“Not a” is always {{kein}}.

practice.q: Which nouns change in the accusative?
practice.why: {{der}} → {{den}}, {{ein}} → {{einen}}; feminine, neuter and plural stay the same.

lessons.title: Order food and drinks
lessons.summary: Order in a café or a restaurant, ask for the check and pay: “I'd like a coffee and a piece of cake, please.”
lessons.topic: {{Ich möchte}}, {{ich hätte gern}}, {{ich nehme}} + the accusative; paying

goal.t: Ich möchte einen Kaffee und ein Stück Kuchen, bitte.
goal.tr: I'd like a coffee and a piece of cake, please.

dialog.t: Guten Tag! Was möchten Sie?
dialog.tr: Hello! What would you like?

dialog.t: Ich hätte gern einen Cappuccino.
dialog.tr: I'd like a cappuccino.

dialog.t: Gern. Und zu essen?
dialog.tr: Sure. And to eat?

dialog.t: Ich nehme den Apfelkuchen.
dialog.tr: I'll have the apple cake.

dialog.t: Mit Sahne?
dialog.tr: With whipped cream?

dialog.t: Ja, bitte. … Zahlen, bitte!
dialog.tr: Yes, please. … The check, please!

dialog.t: Das macht sieben Euro achtzig.
dialog.tr: That's €7.80.

dialog.t: Neun Euro, bitte. Stimmt so.
dialog.tr: Make it nine. Keep the change.

blocks.p: **Three ways to order**, all polite: {{Ich möchte…}} “I'd like…”, {{Ich hätte gern…}} “I'd like…” (very common, a touch more polite), and {{Ich nehme…}} “I'll have…” (when you pick from the menu). Then comes what you want, in the accusative, because it's the object: {{einen Kaffee}}, {{eine Cola}}, {{ein Wasser}}.
{{möchte}} has no {{-t}} with {{er}} or {{sie}}: {{ich möchte}}, {{du möchtest}}, {{er/sie möchte}}, {{wir/sie/Sie möchten}}, {{ihr möchtet}}.

**Paying.** Say {{Zahlen, bitte!}} or {{Die Rechnung, bitte!}} “The check, please!” The server may ask {{Zusammen oder getrennt?}} “Together or separately?” In Germany you usually pay at the table, and you tip by saying the total you want to pay ({{Neun Euro, bitte.}}) or, when you hand over the exact amount you want to give, just {{Stimmt so.}} “Keep the change.”

ex.t: Ich hätte gern ein Glas Wasser.
ex.tr: I'd like a glass of water.

ex.t: Ich nehme die Suppe und einen Salat.
ex.tr: I'll have the soup and a salad.
What would you like to drink?
An orange juice for me, please.

blocks.tip: {{Gern}} from a server means “Sure, with pleasure”. And when the food comes, they'll often say {{Guten Appetit!}}: you can answer {{Danke!}}

mistakes.why: {{der Kaffee}} is masculine and it's the object (what you want): {{einen}}.
{{möchte}} has no ending with {{er}} or {{sie}}.

practice.tr: I'd like a water.

Ich hätte gern ein Tee, bitte.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.summary: Say what you like doing, and which things and people you like: “I like drinking coffee, but I don't like tea.”
lessons.topic: {{gern}} after the verb; {{mögen}}; {{mich, dich, ihn, sie, es}}

goal.t: Ich trinke gern Kaffee, aber ich mag keinen Tee.
goal.tr: I like drinking coffee, but I don't like tea.

dialog.t: Was machst du gern?
dialog.tr: What do you like to do?

dialog.t: Ich lese gern und ich koche gern. Und du?
dialog.tr: I like reading and cooking. And you?

dialog.t: Ich spiele gern Fußball. Magst du Fußball?
dialog.tr: I like playing soccer. Do you like soccer?

dialog.t: Nein, nicht so. Aber ich mag Tennis.
dialog.tr: No, not really. But I like tennis.

dialog.t: Kennst du Jonas? Er spielt auch Tennis.
dialog.tr: Do you know Jonas? He plays tennis too.

dialog.t: Ja, ich kenne ihn. Ich mag ihn sehr!
dialog.tr: Yes, I know him. I like him a lot!

blocks.p: **gern: liking what you do.** To say you like *doing* something, say that you do it and add {{gern}} after the verb: {{Ich koche.}} “I cook.” → {{Ich koche gern.}} “I like cooking.” For “don't like”: {{nicht gern}}: {{Ich koche nicht gern.}}
**mögen: liking things and people.** For a thing or a person, use {{mögen}}, with the accusative (what you like is the object): {{Ich mag Pizza.}} {{Ich mag den Film.}} {{Ich mag keinen Tee.}}
**me, you, him, her.** People and things you like or know are objects, so pronouns take the accusative too. Of “he, she, it”, only {{er}} changes ({{ihn}}); “me”, “you” and “us” have their own forms:

ex.tr: Do you like playing the guitar?

ex.t: Der Film? Ich mag ihn nicht.
ex.tr: The movie? I don't like it.

blocks.tip: {{Gern!}} or {{Gerne!}} on its own is a friendly answer: “Sure, I'd love to!”, and also “You're welcome” after someone says {{Danke}}.

mistakes.why: {{gern}} comes after the verb: the verb stays second.
He's the object here, so {{er}} becomes {{ihn}}.

practice.why: The verb in second place, then {{gern}}.

practice.t: Der Kuchen ist super. Ich mag ___!
practice.tr: The cake is great. I like it!
practice.why: {{der Kuchen}} is masculine, and here it's the object: {{ihn}}.

practice.tr: Do you like dogs?
practice.why: With {{du}}: {{magst}}, first in a yes/no question.

practice.tr: I don't like coffee.
practice.why: {{der Kaffee}} with no article, as an object: “not any” is {{keinen}}.

practice.tr: Do you like playing soccer?

options: Ja, ich kenne sie. Sie ist sehr nett.
Ja, ich kenne ihr. Sie ist sehr nett.
lines.why: “Her” as an object is {{sie}}, the same as “she”.

answers.t: Ich koche gern und ich tanze sehr gern. Ich mag keine Spinnen.

lessons.title: Talk about your family
lessons.summary: Say who's in your family, what their names are and what they do: “My sister's name is Julia.”
lessons.topic: {{mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr}} (and {{meinen}} for the object); {{Annas}} “Anna's”

goal.t: Meine Schwester heißt Julia und wohnt in München.
goal.tr: My sister's name is Julia and she lives in Munich.

dialog.t: Wer ist das?
dialog.tr: Who's that?

dialog.t: Das ist meine Mutter, und das ist mein Vater.
dialog.tr: That's my mother, and that's my father.

dialog.t: Und wer ist der Junge?
dialog.tr: And who's the boy?

dialog.t: Das ist mein Bruder Paul. Und das ist seine Freundin.
dialog.tr: That's my brother Paul. And that's his girlfriend.

dialog.t: Wie heißt sie?
dialog.tr: What's her name?

dialog.t: Keine Ahnung! Er hat jeden Monat eine neue.
dialog.tr: No idea! He has a new one every month.

blocks.p: **my, your, his…** These words go in front of a noun and take the same endings as {{ein}}: no ending for masculine and neuter nouns, {{-e}} for feminine and plural ones.

**His or her?** That depends on the owner, not on the thing: {{sein}} when the owner is a man, {{ihr}} when it's a woman (or several people). Then the ending follows the thing owned: Paul's girlfriend is {{seine Freundin}}; Julia's husband is {{ihr Mann}}.
**As objects**, they change just like {{ein}}: a masculine noun adds {{-en}}. {{Ich besuche meinen Vater.}} “I'm visiting my father.” {{Kennst du meinen Bruder?}} “Do you know my brother?”
**Anna's.** With names, German adds {{-s}}, with no apostrophe: {{Annas Bruder}} “Anna's brother”, {{Pauls Auto}} “Paul's car”. In speech you'll also hear {{der Bruder von Anna}}.

ex.t: Unsere Kinder sind sieben und neun.
ex.tr: Our children are seven and nine.

ex.t: Ich besuche am Sonntag meinen Opa.
ex.tr: I'm visiting my grandpa on Sunday.

ex.note: polite, at a reception desk, for example

blocks.tip: Family words come in useful groups: {{die Eltern}} “parents”, {{die Geschwister}} “brothers and sisters”, {{die Großeltern}} “grandparents”, whom most people call {{Oma}} and {{Opa}}.

mistakes.why: {{die Mutter}} is feminine: {{meine}}.

mistakes.wrong: Julia und sein Mann wohnen in Köln.
mistakes.right: Julia und ihr Mann wohnen in Köln.
mistakes.tr: Julia and her husband live in Cologne.
mistakes.why: The owner is Julia, a woman: {{ihr}}.
{{der Vater}} is a masculine object here: {{meinen}}.

practice.why: Paul is the owner: {{sein-}}; {{die Schwester}} is feminine: {{-e}}.

I'm visiting my parents.

lessons.title: Say what you want to do
lessons.summary: Say what you'd like to do and what you want to do: “I'd like to go to the movies tonight.” Your first verb bracket.
lessons.topic: {{möchten}} and {{wollen}} + an infinitive at the end (the verb bracket)

goal.t: Ich möchte heute Abend ins Kino gehen.
goal.tr: I'd like to go to the movies tonight.

dialog.t: Was möchtest du am Wochenende machen?
dialog.tr: What would you like to do on the weekend?

dialog.t: Ich möchte lange schlafen!
dialog.tr: I'd like to sleep late!

dialog.t: Und dann? Wir wollen wandern. Willst du auch kommen?
dialog.tr: And then? We want to go hiking. Do you want to come too?

dialog.t: Wo wollt ihr wandern?
dialog.tr: Where do you want to hike?

dialog.t: Im Harz.
dialog.tr: In the Harz mountains.

dialog.t: Super, ich komme!
dialog.tr: Great, I'm in!

blocks.means: a helping verb that says how you stand toward an action: want to, would like to, can, must, may.

blocks.p: **Two verbs, two places.** {{möchten}} “would like” and {{wollen}} “want” take the usual verb place, second, and change for the person. The verb that says what you want *to do* goes to the **very end**, as an infinitive: {{Ich möchte heute Abend ins Kino gehen.}}, word for word “I would like tonight to the cinema go.”

blocks.means: the two parts of a German verb that frame a sentence: one in second place, the other at the very end.

blocks.p: **möchten or wollen?** {{möchten}} is “would like”: soft and polite, right for asking and offering. {{wollen}} is “want”: direct, fine among friends and for firm plans, but a bit blunt in a shop. And careful: {{ich will}} means “I want”, never “I will”.

ex.tr: Do you want to have a coffee?

ex.t: Wir wollen im Sommer nach Italien fahren.
ex.tr: We want to go to Italy in the summer.
What would you like to order?
Would you like to eat with us?

blocks.tip: Where's the “to”? German doesn't need one here: {{Ich möchte schlafen.}} is “I'd like to sleep.”

mistakes.tr: I'd like to go to the movies.
mistakes.why: The second verb goes to the very end.
No {{zu}} after {{möchten}} or {{wollen}}, and the infinitive goes last.
{{will}} means “want”, not “will”. For the future, German usually just uses the present with a time word.

practice.tr: I'd like to go to the movies tonight.
What do you want to do on the weekend?

practice.t: Wir möchten im Sommer nach Spanien ___.
practice.tr: We'd like to go to Spain in the summer.

practice.q: A friend makes plans with you.

lines.t: Möchtest du heute Abend essen gehen?
lines.tr: Would you like to go out to eat tonight?

options: Ja, gern! Ich möchte Pizza essen.

lines.why: The infinitive {{essen}} goes to the end.

options: Nein, ich mag ihn nicht so.

answers.tr: I'd like to sleep late this weekend.

answers.tr: This year I want to go to Berlin and learn German.

lessons.title: Say what you can do and ask if you may
lessons.summary: Say what you can do, ask for help and ask for permission: “Can I pay by card?”
lessons.topic: {{können}} “can” and {{dürfen}} “may, be allowed to”

goal.t: Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?
goal.tr: Can I pay by card?

dialog.t: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir helfen?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, can you help me?

dialog.t: Ja, natürlich.
dialog.tr: Yes, of course.

dialog.t: Ich suche eine Jacke. Darf ich diese hier anprobieren?
dialog.tr: I'm looking for a jacket. May I try this one on?

dialog.t: Ja, klar. Die Kabine ist dort hinten.
dialog.tr: Yes, sure. The fitting room is back there.

dialog.t: Ich nehme sie. Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?
dialog.tr: I'll take it. Can I pay by card?

dialog.t: Ja, das geht.
dialog.tr: Yes, that's fine.

blocks.p: **können** is “can”: what you're able to do ({{Ich kann schwimmen.}} “I can swim.”) and what's possible ({{Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?}}). **dürfen** is “may, be allowed to”: permission ({{Darf ich hier sitzen?}} “May I sit here?”). Both are modal verbs like {{möchten}}: the modal second, the infinitive at the end.
**Asking for help** is a yes/no question, so the modal comes first: {{Können Sie mir helfen?}} “Can you help me?”, {{Kannst du das bitte wiederholen?}} “Can you repeat that, please?”

**Not allowed.** {{nicht dürfen}} is “mustn't, not be allowed to”: {{Hier darf man nicht parken.}} “You can't park here.” {{man}} means “one, you, people in general”, and takes the {{er}} form of the verb.

ex.t: Ich kann ein bisschen Deutsch sprechen.
ex.tr: I can speak a little German.

ex.t: Kann man hier mit Karte zahlen?
ex.tr: Can you pay by card here?

blocks.tip: {{Ich kann Deutsch.}} on its own means “I speak German”: with a language, {{sprechen}} is understood.

mistakes.why: The infinitive goes to the very end; everything else comes before it.
No {{zu}} after a modal verb.
Not knowing how is {{nicht können}}. {{nicht dürfen}} means you're not allowed.

practice.q: At a pool, a sign says {{Hier darf man nicht springen.}} It means…
options: You're not allowed to jump here.
You're not able to jump here.

practice.tr: Can you help me?
practice.why: With {{Sie}}: {{können}}, first in a yes/no question.

practice.tr: May I sit here?
I can speak a little German.

practice.q: In a shop: you want to pay.

options: Kein Problem. Ich habe zwanzig Euro.
Nicht Problem. Ich habe zwanzig Euro.

answers.tr: I can cook well and play the guitar, but I can't swim.

lessons.title: Say what you have to do
lessons.summary: Say what you have to do, what you don't have to do, and what you're supposed to do: “I can't come today. I have to work.”
lessons.topic: {{müssen}} “must, have to” and {{sollen}} “should”; {{nicht müssen}} = “don't have to”

goal.t: Ich kann heute nicht kommen. Ich muss arbeiten.
goal.tr: I can't come today. I have to work.

dialog.t: Kommst du heute Abend zur Party?
dialog.tr: Are you coming to the party tonight?

dialog.t: Leider nicht. Ich muss für die Prüfung lernen.
dialog.tr: Unfortunately not. I have to study for the exam.

dialog.t: Schade! Und morgen?
dialog.tr: Too bad! And tomorrow?

dialog.t: Ich muss morgen nicht lernen. Wir können ins Kino gehen!
dialog.tr: I don't have to study tomorrow. We can go to the movies!

dialog.t: Gute Idee! Aber ich soll um zehn zu Hause sein.
dialog.tr: Good idea! But I'm supposed to be home at ten.

blocks.p: **müssen** is “must, have to”: {{Ich muss arbeiten.}} It builds the same bracket as the other modal verbs: {{muss}} second, the infinitive at the end.
**Watch out: nicht müssen means “don't have to”**, not “mustn't”. {{Du musst nicht kommen.}} means “You don't have to come” (it's up to you). For “mustn't”, German uses {{nicht dürfen}}:

table: You mustn't come. You're not allowed to come.

blocks.p: **sollen** is “should, be supposed to”: what someone else wants you to do. {{Der Arzt sagt, ich soll mehr schlafen.}} “The doctor says I should sleep more.” And {{Soll ich…?}} offers help: {{Soll ich das Fenster aufmachen?}} “Shall I open the window?”

ex.tr: Do you have to work tomorrow?

ex.t: Wir müssen um acht am Bahnhof sein.
ex.tr: We have to be at the station at eight.
You don't have to wait here.

blocks.tip: {{Ich muss mal.}} on its own, said with a meaningful look, means “I need to go to the bathroom.”

mistakes.why: The infinitive goes last.
{{nicht müssen}} is “don't have to”. For “mustn't”, use {{nicht dürfen}}.

practice.tr: I have to work early tomorrow.
You mustn't park here.
Do you have to work tomorrow?

lessons.summary: Tell the time, say on which day and at what time things happen, and start a sentence with the time: “On Monday I work until six.”
lessons.topic: Clock times; {{um}}, {{am}}, {{im}}; a time word first, with the verb still second

blocks.p: **What time is it?** {{Wie spät ist es?}} or {{Wie viel Uhr ist es?}} The answer: {{Es ist drei Uhr.}} “It's three o'clock.” In everyday speech:
**halb looks ahead** to the next hour: {{halb vier}} is 3:30, halfway to four. On timetables and in anything official, Germans use the 24-hour clock: {{15:30}} is {{fünfzehn Uhr dreißig}}.

**um, am, im.** {{um}} for clock times ({{um acht}} “at eight”), {{am}} for days and parts of the day ({{am Montag}}, {{am Wochenende}}, {{am Abend}}), {{im}} for months and seasons ({{im Juli}}, {{im Sommer}}). And no little word at all with {{heute}} “today”, {{morgen}} “tomorrow” or {{jetzt}} “now”.

**A time word first: the verb stays second.** German sentences often start with the time. The verb keeps its second place, so the subject moves behind it: {{Ich arbeite am Montag.}} → {{Am Montag arbeite ich.}}, word for word “On Monday work I.” It's the verb-second rule again: the time takes first place, and the verb doesn't budge.

ex.t: Der Zug fährt um zehn nach acht.
ex.tr: The train leaves at ten after eight.

ex.t: Im Sommer fahren wir nach Spanien.
ex.tr: In the summer we're going to Spain.

ex.t: Wann beginnt der Film? – Um Viertel nach acht.
ex.tr: When does the movie start? – At a quarter after eight.
On the weekend I sleep late.

blocks.tip: The days: {{Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag, Freitag, Samstag, Sonntag}}. They're all masculine, so “on Monday” is {{am Montag}}; “on Mondays” is {{montags}}.

{{halb}} looks ahead: 7:30 is halfway to eight, {{halb acht}}. ({{halb sieben}} is 6:30.)

lessons.title: Describe your daily routine
lessons.summary: Say what you do every day, from getting up to going to bed: “I get up at seven every day.”
lessons.topic: Separable verbs ({{aufstehen}}, {{einkaufen}}, {{anrufen}}): the little front part goes to the end

goal.t: Ich stehe jeden Tag um sieben Uhr auf.

blocks.means: a verb with a small front part (like {{an}}, {{auf}} or {{ein}}) that splits off in a sentence and goes to the very end.

blocks.p: **A verb in two pieces.** Many everyday verbs have a little front part: {{aufstehen}} “to get up” ({{auf}} “up” + {{stehen}} “stand”), {{einkaufen}} “to go shopping”, {{anrufen}} “to call”. In a sentence, the main part takes the verb's place (second) and the front part goes to the **very end**: {{Ich stehe um sieben auf.}} It's the verb bracket again, as in {{Ich möchte … gehen.}}

table: She watches TV in the evening.

blocks.p: **After a modal verb, it stays in one piece.** When the verb is the infinitive at the end, its two parts are written together: {{Ich muss um sechs aufstehen.}} {{Kannst du mich anrufen?}}
**Which verbs split?** You can hear it: the front part is stressed: {{AUFstehen}}, {{EINkaufen}}, {{ANrufen}}. Common front parts are {{an, auf, aus, ein, mit, zu, ab, fern, zurück}}.

ex.t: Der Zug kommt um acht an.
Machst du bitte das Fenster zu?
ex.tr: Could you close the window, please?
I have to get up early tomorrow.

blocks.tip: {{fangen}} becomes {{fängt}} and {{sehen}} becomes {{sieht}} with {{er}} or {{sie}}: some verbs change their vowel. That's the next lesson.

mistakes.tr: I have to get up at six.

goal.t: Mein Bruder fährt gern Rad und meine Schwester liest viel.

blocks.p: **Same endings, different vowel.** Some very common verbs change their main vowel, but only with {{du}} and {{er/sie/es}}. The endings stay regular, and the other persons are completely normal.

The common ones. Like {{fahren}}: {{schlafen}} “sleep” ({{er schläft}}), {{laufen}} “run” ({{er läuft}}: {{au}} → {{äu}}), {{tragen}} “wear, carry”. Like {{sprechen}}: {{essen}} “eat” ({{er isst}}), {{nehmen}} “take” ({{er nimmt}}), {{helfen}} “help” ({{er hilft}}), {{treffen}} “meet” ({{er trifft}}), {{geben}} “give” ({{er gibt}}). Like {{lesen}}: {{sehen}} “see” ({{er sieht}}).
Dictionaries mark these verbs, and you'll hear them so often that the right form soon sounds right. For now: if a verb sounds odd with {{du}} or {{er}}, check whether its vowel changes.

ex.t: Sie trifft am Freitag ihre Freundinnen.
ex.tr: She's meeting her friends on Friday.

blocks.tip: {{Rad fahren}} or {{Fahrrad fahren}} is “to ride a bike”, {{Ski fahren}} “to ski”. And {{fahren}} is any going by vehicle: {{Ich fahre nach Berlin.}} “I'm going to Berlin” (by car, train or bus).

lessons.topic: {{es gibt}} + the accusative; {{Wo ist…?}}; the {{Sie}} command; {{links, rechts, geradeaus}}

goal.t: Entschuldigung, gibt es hier in der Nähe eine Apotheke?

blocks.p: **Is there…? es gibt.** {{es gibt}} means “there is” and “there are”. The thing that exists is its object, so it's in the accusative, and a masculine noun gets {{einen}}: {{Gibt es hier einen Supermarkt?}} “Is there a supermarket here?”, {{Es gibt keinen Bus.}} “There's no bus.” It never changes for the plural: {{Es gibt zwei Bahnhöfe.}}
**Where is…?** For something you know exists, ask {{Wo ist…?}}: {{Wo ist der Bahnhof?}} “Where's the station?”, {{Wo sind die Toiletten?}} “Where are the restrooms?”

blocks.means: the form of a verb for telling someone what to do: Go! Take the bus!

blocks.p: **Telling a stranger what to do: the Sie command.** Take the {{Sie}} form and put the verb first, then {{Sie}}: {{Gehen Sie geradeaus.}} “Go straight ahead.”, {{Nehmen Sie den Bus.}} “Take the bus.” It looks like a question, but your voice goes down. With {{bitte}}, it's polite: {{Warten Sie bitte hier.}} “Please wait here.”

lessons.title: Tell someone what to do
lessons.summary: Give friends instructions and tips (“Come in! Have a piece of cake!”), and make them friendly with doch and mal.
lessons.topic: The command with {{du}} and {{ihr}}; {{doch}}, {{mal}} and {{bitte}}

blocks.p: **To a friend (du):** take the {{du}} form and drop the {{-st}} (and the {{du}}): {{du kommst}} → {{Komm!}}, {{du machst}} → {{Mach!}} Verbs that change {{e}} to {{i}} keep the {{i}} ({{du nimmst}} → {{Nimm!}}, {{Iss!}}, {{Lies!}}), but verbs that change {{a}} to {{ä}} lose the dots ({{du fährst}} → {{Fahr!}}).

**To two or more friends (ihr):** just the {{ihr}} form, without {{ihr}}: {{ihr kommt}} → {{Kommt!}}, {{ihr macht}} → {{Macht!}} **To strangers (Sie):** as in the last lesson, {{Kommen Sie!}} And separable verbs send their front part to the end, as always: {{Komm rein!}} {{Mach das Licht aus!}}

**Making it friendly: doch, mal, bitte.** A bare command can sound bossy, so Germans soften it with little words: {{doch}} “go on, why don't you”, {{mal}} “just, for a moment”, {{bitte}} “please”. {{Komm doch mit!}} “Why don't you come along!”, {{Sag mal…}} “Tell me…”, {{Hilf mir bitte mal.}} “Could you give me a hand?”

blocks.tip: Verbs whose stem ends in {{-t}} or {{-d}} keep an {{-e}} in the {{du}} command: {{Warte!}}, {{Antworte!}} “Answer!”. And {{bitte}} can go almost anywhere: {{Bitte komm!}}, {{Komm bitte!}}

lessons.title: Say what you did
lessons.summary: Say what you did yesterday or last weekend: “On the weekend I played soccer and cooked.”
lessons.topic: The Perfekt: {{haben}} + a participle {{ge-…-t}} ({{gespielt}}, {{gekauft}}, {{gearbeitet}})

goal.t: Am Wochenende habe ich Fußball gespielt und gekocht.
goal.tr: On the weekend I played soccer and cooked.

blocks.means: the form of a verb used with {{haben}} or {{sein}} to talk about the past: {{gemacht}} “done, made”, {{gespielt}} “played”.
the past tense Germans use in conversation: {{haben}} or {{sein}}, plus a participle: {{ich habe gespielt}} “I played, I have played”.

blocks.p: **The past in conversation.** When Germans talk about what happened, they almost always use the Perfekt: a form of {{haben}} in second place, and a participle at the very end. Another verb bracket: {{Ich habe Fußball gespielt.}}, word for word “I have soccer played.”
**One form, two English meanings.** {{Ich habe gespielt}} is both “I played” and “I have played”, and it's fine with a time word: {{Gestern habe ich Tennis gespielt.}} “Yesterday I played tennis.”

**Regular participles: ge- + stem + -t.** Take the infinitive, drop {{-en}}, put {{ge-}} in front and {{-t}} at the end: {{spielen}} → {{gespielt}}, {{machen}} → {{gemacht}}, {{kaufen}} → {{gekauft}}. If the stem ends in {{-t}} or {{-d}}, it's {{-et}}: {{arbeiten}} → {{gearbeitet}}.

**Questions and “not”** work as always: {{haben}} goes first in a yes/no question ({{Hast du Brot gekauft?}}) and after a question word ({{Was hast du gemacht?}}); {{nicht}} goes just before the participle ({{Ich habe nicht gearbeitet.}}).

ex.t: Wir haben im Urlaub viel gelacht.
ex.tr: We laughed a lot on vacation.

ex.t: Er hat zwei Jahre in Wien gewohnt.

blocks.p: **The most common verbs have participles in -en**, often with a different vowel: {{essen}} → {{gegessen}}, {{trinken}} → {{getrunken}}, {{sehen}} → {{gesehen}}. They're the verbs you use most, so learn each one as you meet it; dictionaries list them.

Patterns help: {{ei}} often becomes {{ie}} ({{schreiben}} → {{geschrieben}}), {{i}} often becomes {{u}} ({{trinken}} → {{getrunken}}, {{finden}} → {{gefunden}}), and some verbs keep their vowel ({{gegessen}}, {{gesehen}}, {{gelesen}}, {{geschlafen}}). Everything else stays the same: {{haben}} second, the participle at the end.

lessons.topic: The Perfekt with {{sein}}: moving and changing ({{gefahren}}, {{gegangen}}, {{gekommen}}), and {{geblieben}}

goal.t: Wir sind nach Rom geflogen und eine Woche geblieben.

blocks.p: **Some verbs use sein, not haben.** Verbs of **moving from one place to another** ({{gehen}}, {{fahren}}, {{fliegen}}, {{kommen}}) and of **changing state** ({{aufstehen}} “get up”, {{einschlafen}} “fall asleep”) make their Perfekt with {{sein}}: {{Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren.}} “I went to Berlin.” Two more take {{sein}} although nothing moves: {{bleiben}} “stay” ({{ich bin geblieben}}) and {{sein}} itself ({{ich bin gewesen}}).

**The rest is the same:** {{sein}} in second place, changing for the person ({{ich bin}}, {{du bist}}, {{wir sind}}…), the participle at the end. Almost all of these verbs have participles in {{-en}}.
A useful test: if you can ask “where to?”, or the verb means a change of state, it's probably {{sein}}. Everything else, including {{essen}}, {{schlafen}} and {{arbeiten}}, takes {{haben}}.

ex.t: Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen.
ex.tr: I went to the movies yesterday.

Wir sind am Sonntag zu Hause geblieben.

lessons.title: Tell someone about your day
lessons.summary: Tell what you did today, with everyday verbs like get up, call, shop, visit and forget: “I got up early and called my mother.”
lessons.topic: Participles of separable verbs ({{aufgestanden}}, {{angerufen}}) and of verbs without {{ge-}} ({{besucht}}, {{verstanden}}, {{telefoniert}})

goal.t: Heute bin ich früh aufgestanden und habe meine Mutter angerufen.
goal.tr: Today I got up early and called my mother.

dialog.t: Wie war dein Tag?
dialog.tr: How was your day?

dialog.t: Anstrengend! Ich bin um sechs aufgestanden.
dialog.tr: Exhausting! I got up at six.

dialog.t: Oh je. Und dann?
dialog.tr: Oh dear. And then?

dialog.t: Ich habe den ganzen Tag telefoniert. Dann habe ich eingekauft und Oma besucht.

dialog.tr: Oh no, I forgot!

blocks.p: **Separable verbs: ge- goes in the middle.** The front part stays in front, and {{ge}} goes between it and the rest: {{einkaufen}} → {{eingekauft}}, {{anrufen}} → {{angerufen}}, {{aufstehen}} → {{aufgestanden}}. It's written as one word, at the end, as usual: {{Ich habe eingekauft.}}

**No ge- at all** for two kinds of verb. First, verbs that begin with an unstressed front part that never splits off: {{be-}}, {{ver-}}, {{er-}}, {{ent-}}: {{besuchen}} → {{besucht}}, {{verstehen}} → {{verstanden}}, {{erklären}} → {{erklärt}}. Second, verbs ending in {{-ieren}}: {{telefonieren}} → {{telefoniert}}, {{studieren}} → {{studiert}}.
So a participle tells you what kind of verb it is: {{ge}} in the middle means a separable verb; no {{ge}} at all means a {{be-}}, {{ver-}} or {{-ieren}} verb (or one like them).

ex.tr: When did you get up today?

ex.t: Wir haben unsere Freunde in Hamburg besucht.
ex.tr: We visited our friends in Hamburg.

ex.t: Entschuldigung, ich habe Sie nicht verstanden.

ex.tr: I went to college in Berlin.

blocks.tip: An apology to keep handy: {{Entschuldigung, das habe ich vergessen.}} “Sorry, I forgot.”

lessons.title: Say how it was
lessons.summary: Say how things were, and what you had, could or had to do: “The party was great, but I had to go home early.”
lessons.topic: {{war}} and {{hatte}}; {{konnte, musste, wollte, durfte}}: the simple past of {{sein}}, {{haben}} and the modal verbs

goal.t: Die Party war toll, aber ich musste früh nach Hause gehen.
goal.tr: The party was great, but I had to go home early.

dialog.t: Wie war dein Urlaub?
dialog.tr: How was your vacation?

dialog.t: Super! Das Wetter war schön und das Hotel war direkt am Meer.
dialog.tr: Great! The weather was nice and the hotel was right by the sea.

blocks.p: **war, hatte: the exception everyone uses.** For {{sein}} and {{haben}}, Germans rarely say {{ich bin gewesen}} or {{ich habe gehabt}} in conversation. They use a one-word past: {{ich war}} “I was”, {{ich hatte}} “I had”. The same goes for the modal verbs: {{ich konnte}} “I could”, {{ich musste}} “I had to”, {{ich wollte}} “I wanted to”.

blocks.means: the one-word past tense: {{ich war}}, {{ich hatte}}. In conversation it's used mostly for {{sein}}, {{haben}} and the modal verbs; in books and stories, for every verb.

blocks.p: {{ich}} and {{er/sie}} share one form, with no ending. The modal verbs lose their dots: {{können}} → {{konnte}}, {{müssen}} → {{musste}}, {{dürfen}} → {{durfte}}; and {{wollen}} → {{wollte}}. ({{möchten}} has no past of its own: use {{wollte}}.)
**With a modal, it's still a bracket**: the modal in second place, the infinitive at the end: {{Ich musste früh gehen.}} {{Wir konnten nicht kommen.}}

ex.t: Ich war krank und hatte Fieber.
ex.tr: I was sick and had a fever.

ex.t: Ich wollte dich anrufen, aber ich konnte nicht.
ex.tr: I wanted to call you, but I couldn't.

ex.t: Als Kind durfte ich nicht viel fernsehen.
ex.tr: As a child I wasn't allowed to watch much TV.

blocks.tip: So a typical German story mixes the two pasts: {{Ich war in Berlin und habe viele Museen besucht.}} “I was in Berlin and visited lots of museums.” That's exactly how people talk.

mistakes.why: {{sein}} never takes {{haben}}; and in conversation people simply say {{war}}.
Still a bracket: the infinitive goes last.
With {{wir}}: {{waren}}. {{wart}} is for {{ihr}}.

lessons.title: Say how and where you travel
lessons.summary: Say how you get around and where you're going: “I take the bus to work.” Meet the dative, the form after mit, zu and bei.
lessons.topic: The dative after {{mit, zu, bei, nach, aus, von, seit}}: {{dem, der, den…-n}}; {{zum}}, {{zur}}, {{beim}}

goal.t: Ich fahre mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.
goal.tr: I take the bus to work.

dialog.t: Wie kommst du zur Arbeit?
dialog.tr: How do you get to work?

dialog.t: Mit dem Fahrrad. Und du?
dialog.tr: By bike. And you?

dialog.t: Mit der U-Bahn. Aber heute fahre ich nach der Arbeit zu meiner Schwester.
dialog.tr: By subway. But today after work I'm going to my sister's.

dialog.t: Wohnt sie weit weg?
dialog.tr: Does she live far away?

dialog.t: Nein, nur zehn Minuten von hier.
dialog.tr: No, just ten minutes from here.

blocks.means: a little word that says where, when or how: in, on, with, to, from.
the form German uses after certain prepositions, like {{mit}} “with” and {{zu}} “to”, and for the person who receives something.

blocks.p: **After mit, zu and friends: the dative.** Some prepositions are always followed by the dative. The seven you need most: {{mit}} “with, by”, {{zu}} “to (a person or a place)”, {{bei}} “at (someone's place, a company)”, {{nach}} “to (a city, a country), after”, {{aus}} “from, out of”, {{von}} “from, of”, {{seit}} “since, for”.

**The dative changes every article:** {{der}} and {{das}} become {{dem}}, {{die}} becomes {{der}}, and the plural {{die}} becomes {{den}}, with an {{-n}} on the noun too. {{ein}}, {{kein}} and {{mein}} follow: {{einem}}, {{einer}}, {{meinem}}, {{meiner}}, {{meinen}}.

**Short forms.** Spoken and written German joins some of them: {{zu dem}} → {{zum}}, {{zu der}} → {{zur}}, {{bei dem}} → {{beim}}, {{von dem}} → {{vom}}: {{zum Bahnhof}}, {{zur Arbeit}}, {{beim Arzt}} “at the doctor's”.

**Going to a place:** {{nach}} for cities and countries ({{nach Berlin}}, {{nach Spanien}}) and for going home ({{nach Hause}}); {{zu}} for people, buildings and events ({{zu meiner Mutter}}, {{zum Supermarkt}}, {{zur Party}}). And being somewhere: {{zu Hause}} “at home”, {{bei meiner Mutter}} “at my mother's”.

ex.t: Wir fahren mit dem Zug nach München.
ex.tr: We're taking the train to Munich.

ex.t: Heute Abend bin ich bei meinen Eltern.
Ich komme gerade aus dem Büro.
ex.tr: I'm just coming from the office.

ex.t: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr in Hamburg.
ex.tr: I've lived in Hamburg for a year.

blocks.tip: {{zu Fuß}} “on foot” is the one way of getting around without {{mit}}: {{Ich gehe zu Fuß.}} “I'm walking.”

Cities and countries take {{nach}}.
Dative plural: {{den}}, and {{-n}} on the noun.

lessons.title: Give and send things to people
lessons.summary: Say who you give, send or show things to: “I'm giving my mother flowers for her birthday.”
lessons.topic: The dative for the person who receives: {{dem, der, den}}; {{mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, Ihnen}}

goal.t: Ich schenke meiner Mutter Blumen zum Geburtstag.
goal.tr: I'm giving my mother flowers for her birthday.

dialog.t: Was schenkst du deinem Vater zum Geburtstag?
dialog.tr: What are you giving your dad for his birthday?

dialog.t: Ich weiß nicht. Vielleicht ein Buch. Hast du eine Idee?
dialog.tr: I don't know. Maybe a book. Any ideas?

dialog.t: Schenk ihm doch Konzertkarten!
dialog.tr: Why don't you give him concert tickets!

dialog.t: Gute Idee! Kannst du mir den Link schicken?
dialog.tr: Good idea! Can you send me the link?

dialog.t: Klar, ich schicke ihn dir gleich.
dialog.tr: Sure, I'll send it to you right away.

blocks.p: **Two objects.** Verbs like {{geben}} “give”, {{schenken}} “give as a present”, {{schicken}} “send”, {{zeigen}} “show”, {{erklären}} “explain” and {{bringen}} “bring” have two objects: the thing (accusative) and the person who gets it (dative). {{Ich gebe dem Kellner das Geld.}} “I give the waiter the money.” The person usually comes first, just like English “give *the waiter* the money”.
**When the thing is a pronoun too, it goes first:** {{Ich gebe es dir.}} “I'll give it to you.”, {{Kannst du ihn mir zeigen?}} “Can you show it to me?”
These dative pronouns are also what you use after {{mit}}, {{zu}} and {{bei}}: {{mit mir}} “with me”, {{zu dir}} “to your place”, {{bei uns}} “at our place”.

ex.t: Kannst du mir das Salz geben?
ex.tr: Can you pass me the salt?

ex.t: Wir schicken unseren Freunden eine Postkarte.
ex.tr: We're sending our friends a postcard.

ex.t: Er erklärt den Kindern das Spiel.
ex.tr: He's explaining the game to the children.

ex.t: Bringen Sie mir bitte die Rechnung.

blocks.tip: {{Wie geht es dir?}} “How are you?” literally asks “How goes it to you?”: {{dir}} is dative. To a stranger: {{Wie geht es Ihnen?}} And the answer: {{Mir geht es gut, danke.}}

mistakes.why: The person who receives is in the dative: {{dir}}, not {{dich}}.

When the thing is a pronoun, it comes first.

lessons.title: Say what you like and how you feel
lessons.summary: Say that something pleases you, tastes good or fits, and say how you feel: “I like the jacket, but it doesn't fit me.”
lessons.topic: Verbs with the dative: {{gefallen, schmecken, passen, gehören, helfen}}; {{Mir ist kalt.}}

goal.t: Die Jacke gefällt mir, aber sie passt mir nicht.
goal.tr: I like the jacket, but it doesn't fit me.

dialog.t: Und? Wie gefällt Ihnen die Jacke?
dialog.tr: So? How do you like the jacket?

dialog.t: Die Farbe gefällt mir sehr. Aber sie ist mir zu groß.
dialog.tr: I really like the color. But it's too big for me.

dialog.t: Moment, hier ist sie in S.
dialog.tr: Just a moment, here it is in a small.

dialog.t: Ja, die passt mir!

dialog.t: Sie steht Ihnen super.
dialog.tr: It looks great on you.

dialog.t: Danke! Ich nehme sie.
dialog.tr: Thanks! I'll take it.

blocks.p: **Back to front.** With {{gefallen}}, the thing you like is the subject, and *you* are in the dative: {{Die Jacke gefällt mir.}}, word for word “The jacket pleases me.” So the verb agrees with the thing: {{Die Schuhe gefallen mir.}} “I like the shoes.”
Other everyday verbs work the same way, with the person in the dative:

table: I like the soup (it tastes good to me).
The dress looks good on you!

blocks.p: **How you feel: Mir ist…** For feeling cold, hot or sick, German says “to me it is cold”: {{Mir ist kalt.}} “I'm cold.”, {{Mir ist schlecht.}} “I feel sick.”, {{Mir ist langweilig.}} “I'm bored.” And {{Wie geht es dir? – Mir geht es gut.}} “How are you? – I'm fine.”

**Three kinds of liking.** {{gern}} for what you like doing ({{Ich koche gern.}}), {{mögen}} for things and people in general ({{Ich mag Hunde.}}), {{gefallen}} for something you see, hear or try and like ({{Das Lied gefällt mir.}} “I like this song.”).

lessons.title: Say where things are
lessons.summary: Say where something is: on the table, under the bed, next to the door: “Your phone is on the table in the kitchen.”
lessons.topic: {{in, an, auf, unter, über, neben, vor, hinter, zwischen}} + the dative for “where?”; {{liegen, stehen, hängen}}

goal.t: Dein Handy liegt auf dem Tisch in der Küche.
goal.tr: Your phone is on the table in the kitchen.

dialog.t: Wo ist mein Schlüssel?

dialog.tr: Isn't it on the shelf?

blocks.p: **Where? Nine prepositions with the dative.** To say where something is, use one of these nine words, followed by the dative:

table: {{neben der Tür}} next to the door
{{vor dem Haus}} in front of the house

blocks.p: **Short forms:** {{in dem}} → {{im}}, {{an dem}} → {{am}}: {{im Kühlschrank}} “in the fridge”, {{am Fenster}} “at the window”.

**liegen, stehen, hängen.** Where English just says “is”, German often says how a thing is placed: {{liegen}} “lie” for things lying flat ({{Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.}}), {{stehen}} “stand” for upright things ({{Die Flasche steht im Kühlschrank.}}), {{hängen}} “hang” ({{Das Bild hängt an der Wand.}}). {{sein}} is always fine too, but these sound natural.

ex.tr: The kids are in the yard.
The milk is in the fridge.

ex.t: Wir treffen uns vor dem Kino.
ex.tr: We're meeting in front of the movie theater.

ex.t: Die Apotheke ist neben der Bank.

ex.t: Die Katze schläft unter dem Bett.
ex.tr: The cat is sleeping under the bed.

blocks.tip: {{auf}} or {{an}}? {{auf}} is on top of something flat, {{an}} is on something upright or at an edge: {{auf dem Tisch}}, but {{an der Wand}}, {{am Fenster}}, {{am Meer}} “at the seaside”.

dialog.t: Okay. Und dann gehen wir ins Restaurant. Ich habe Hunger!

blocks.p: **Where? or where to?** The nine prepositions from the last lesson take the dative for *where something is* ({{wo?}}), but the accusative for *where something is going* ({{wohin?}}): {{Das Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.}} (where it is), {{Ich lege das Handy auf den Tisch.}} (where it goes).
**Short forms:** {{in das}} → {{ins}} ({{ins Kino}}, {{ins Bett}}), {{an das}} → {{ans}} ({{ans Meer}}).

**Putting things somewhere: legen, stellen, hängen.** They go with the accusative, and their partners from the last lesson with the dative: you {{legen}} something (put it down flat) and then it {{liegt}}; you {{stellen}} it (stand it up) and then it {{steht}}; you {{hängen}} it and then it {{hängt}}.

table: {{Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.}}
{{Ich stelle die Flasche in den Kühlschrank.}}
{{Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand.}}

blocks.p: **Going places** works the same way: {{Ich gehe ins Kino.}} “I'm going to the movies.” (where to?), {{Ich bin im Kino.}} “I'm at the movies.” (where?).

ex.t: Wir gehen heute Abend ins Theater.
ex.tr: We're going to the theater tonight.

ex.tr: I'm going to the mountains on the weekend.

ex.tr: Put the keys on the table.

ex.t: Die Kinder gehen um acht ins Bett.
ex.tr: The kids go to bed at eight.

ex.t: Wohin fährst du im Sommer? – Ans Meer!
ex.tr: Where are you going in the summer? – To the beach!

ex.t: Ich gehe in die Küche und koche.
ex.tr: I'm going into the kitchen to cook.

blocks.tip: Ask yourself: is it moving to a new place ({{wohin?}}, accusative) or staying where it is ({{wo?}}, dative)? {{Ich gehe in die Küche}} (I go there), but {{Ich koche in der Küche}} (I'm there).

lessons.title: Give reasons
lessons.summary: Say why: “I'm learning German because I'd like to work in Berlin.” And meet the other place a German verb can go: the very end.
lessons.topic: {{weil}} (the verb goes to the end) and {{denn}} (the verb stays second); {{warum?}}

goal.t: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Berlin arbeiten möchte.
goal.tr: I'm learning German because I'd like to work in Berlin.

dialog.t: Warum lernen Sie Deutsch?
dialog.tr: Why are you learning German?

dialog.t: Weil meine Frau aus Deutschland kommt.
dialog.tr: Because my wife is from Germany.

dialog.t: Ach, schön! Und Sie, Maria?
dialog.tr: Oh, how nice! And you, Maria?

dialog.t: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich hier studieren will.
dialog.tr: I'm learning German because I want to study here.

dialog.t: Und Tom?
dialog.tr: And Tom?

dialog.t: Ich bin hier, denn ich mag die Sprache einfach!
dialog.tr: I'm here because I just like the language!

blocks.means: a part of a sentence with its own verb: “I'm learning German” + “because I want to work in Berlin”.
a clause that can't stand on its own and starts with a word like {{weil}} “because”, {{dass}} “that” or {{wenn}} “if”. In German, its verb goes to the very end.

blocks.p: **weil: the verb goes to the end.** {{weil}} “because” starts a clause, and in that clause the verb that would normally be second goes to the **very end**: {{Ich habe keine Zeit.}} → {{…, weil ich keine Zeit habe.}} A comma always comes before {{weil}}.

table: {{…, weil ich in Berlin arbeiten will.}}

blocks.p: Look at the last three. A modal goes after the infinitive ({{arbeiten will}}); a separable verb joins up again ({{aufstehe}}); in the Perfekt, {{haben}} or {{sein}} comes last ({{gearbeitet habe}}). The rule is always the same: the verb that's normally second goes to the very end.

**denn: the same meaning, the normal order.** {{denn}} also means “because”, but it doesn't move anything: the verb stays second. {{Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin müde.}} In conversation {{weil}} is much more common, and only {{weil}} can answer {{warum?}} on its own: {{Warum kommst du nicht? – Weil ich arbeiten muss.}}

ex.t: Ich komme heute nicht, weil ich krank bin.
ex.tr: I'm not coming today because I'm sick.

ex.t: Warum lernst du Deutsch? – Weil ich nach Wien ziehe.
ex.tr: Why are you learning German? – Because I'm moving to Vienna.

ex.t: Wir bleiben zu Hause, weil das Wetter so schlecht ist.
ex.tr: We're staying home because the weather's so bad.

ex.t: Sie ist müde, weil sie schlecht geschlafen hat.
ex.tr: She's tired because she slept badly.

ex.t: Er ruft dich an, weil er eine Frage hat.
ex.tr: He's calling you because he has a question.

ex.t: Ich nehme ein Taxi, denn es regnet.
ex.tr: I'm taking a taxi because it's raining.

blocks.tip: This is the first time a German verb goes to the end of a clause. It comes back with {{dass}}, {{wenn}}, {{ob}} and more, and the rule is the same every time.

mistakes.tr: I'm not coming because I'm sick.
mistakes.why: After {{weil}}, the verb goes to the end.

mistakes.tr: I'm learning German because I want to work in Berlin.
mistakes.why: After {{weil}}, the modal goes to the very end, after the infinitive.

lessons.title: Give your opinion
lessons.summary: Say what you think, believe, hope and know: “I think Berlin is a great city.” And agree or disagree.
lessons.topic: {{Ich finde}}, {{ich glaube}}, {{ich denke}}; {{dass}} (verb last), or no {{dass}} (verb second)

goal.t: Ich finde, dass Berlin eine tolle Stadt ist.
goal.tr: I think Berlin is a great city.

dialog.t: Wie findest du den Film?
dialog.tr: What do you think of the movie?

dialog.t: Ich finde ihn ziemlich langweilig.
dialog.tr: I think it's pretty boring.

dialog.t: Echt? Ich finde, dass die Schauspieler super sind.
dialog.tr: Really? I think the actors are great.

dialog.t: Ja, das stimmt. Aber ich glaube, das Buch ist besser.
dialog.tr: Yes, that's true. But I think the book is better.

dialog.t: Da hast du recht. Das Buch ist immer besser!
dialog.tr: You're right there. The book is always better!

blocks.p: **Three ways to say “I think”.** {{Ich finde…}} gives your judgment of something you know (a movie, a city, an idea): {{Ich finde den Film gut.}} {{Ich glaube…}} “I believe, I guess” is for when you're not sure: {{Ich glaube, er kommt heute nicht.}} {{Ich denke…}} works for both. And {{Wie findest du…?}} asks for someone's opinion.

**dass: “that”, with the verb last.** After {{finden}}, {{glauben}}, {{denken}}, {{wissen}} “know”, {{hoffen}} “hope” and {{sagen}} “say”, you can add a clause with {{dass}} “that”. Like {{weil}}, {{dass}} sends the verb to the end: {{Ich glaube, dass er heute nicht kommt.}}
**Or leave dass out.** As English can drop “that”, German can drop {{dass}}, and then the clause keeps its normal order, verb second. Both are everyday German:

table: {{Ich finde, dass das eine gute Idee ist.}}
{{Ich finde, das ist eine gute Idee.}}

blocks.p: **Agreeing and disagreeing:** {{Das stimmt.}} “That's true.”, {{Da hast du recht.}} “You're right about that.”, {{Ich bin deiner Meinung.}} “I agree with you.”, {{Das finde ich nicht.}} “I don't think so.”, {{Ich bin anderer Meinung.}} “I disagree.”

ex.t: Wie findest du meine neue Frisur?
ex.tr: What do you think of my new haircut?

ex.t: Ich finde Deutsch gar nicht so schwer.
ex.tr: I don't find German that hard at all.

ex.t: Ich glaube, dass der Zug Verspätung hat.
ex.tr: I think the train is late.

ex.t: Ich weiß, dass du müde bist.
Ich hoffe, dass es morgen nicht regnet.
ex.tr: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

ex.t: Meiner Meinung nach ist das zu teuer.
ex.tr: In my opinion, that's too expensive.
ex.note: {{meiner Meinung nach}} takes first place, so the verb comes right after it

blocks.tip: {{wissen}} “to know (a fact)” is irregular: {{ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß, wir wissen}}. For knowing a person or a place, it's {{kennen}}: {{Ich kenne Anna.}}

mistakes.wrong: Ich glaube, dass er kommt heute nicht.
mistakes.right: Ich glaube, dass er heute nicht kommt.
mistakes.tr: I think he isn't coming today.
mistakes.why: After {{dass}}, the verb goes to the end.
“I think so” is {{Ich glaube schon}} or {{Ich denke schon}}.

mistakes.wrong: Ich finde, dass ist eine gute Idee.
mistakes.right: Ich finde, das ist eine gute Idee.
mistakes.tr: I think that's a good idea.
mistakes.why: Here “that” means “this thing”: {{das}}, with one {{s}}. {{dass}}, with {{ss}}, joins two clauses and sends the verb to the end.

lessons.title: Say what happens if
lessons.summary: Talk about conditions and plans: “If the weather's nice, we'll have a barbecue on Saturday.”
lessons.topic: {{wenn}} “if, when” (verb last); a {{wenn}} clause first, then verb, comma, verb

goal.t: Wenn das Wetter schön ist, grillen wir am Samstag.
goal.tr: If the weather's nice, we'll have a barbecue on Saturday.

dialog.t: Was machen wir am Wochenende?
dialog.tr: What are we doing on the weekend?

dialog.t: Wenn es nicht regnet, fahren wir an den See.
dialog.tr: If it doesn't rain, we'll go to the lake.

dialog.t: Und wenn es regnet?
dialog.tr: And if it rains?

dialog.t: Dann gehen wir ins Museum.
dialog.tr: Then we'll go to the museum.

dialog.t: Gut. Ich komme mit, wenn ich nicht arbeiten muss.
dialog.tr: Good. I'll come along if I don't have to work.

dialog.t: Ruf mich an, wenn du es weißt!
dialog.tr: Call me when you know!

blocks.p: **wenn: if.** {{wenn}} starts a condition, and like {{weil}} and {{dass}}, it sends its verb to the end: {{Ich komme mit, wenn ich Zeit habe.}} “I'll come along if I have time.”

**The wenn clause first: verb, comma, verb.** Very often the condition comes first. Then the whole {{wenn}} clause counts as the first thing in the sentence, so the main verb comes straight after it, in second place, before its subject: {{Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich mit.}} Two verbs meet at the comma: {{habe, komme}}.

**wenn also means “when, whenever”**, for things that happen again and again, or in the future: {{Wenn ich nach Hause komme, koche ich.}} “When I get home, I'll cook.” (For one particular time in the past, German uses {{als}}: a later lesson.) And {{dann}} “then” can open the second half, to make it extra clear: {{Wenn es regnet, dann bleiben wir zu Hause.}}

ex.t: Wenn du Hunger hast, mache ich dir ein Brot.
ex.tr: If you're hungry, I'll make you a sandwich.

ex.t: Ich rufe dich an, wenn ich angekommen bin.
ex.tr: I'll call you when I've arrived.

ex.t: Wenn ich müde bin, trinke ich Kaffee.
ex.tr: When I'm tired, I drink coffee.

ex.t: Wenn es morgen regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
ex.tr: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home.

ex.t: Was machst du, wenn du frei hast?
ex.tr: What do you do when you have time off?

ex.t: Wenn Sie Fragen haben, rufen Sie mich an.
ex.tr: If you have any questions, call me.

blocks.tip: German needs no “will” in either half: the present does the job. {{Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.}} “If it rains, we'll stay home.”

mistakes.why: The {{wenn}} clause is the first thing, so the verb comes next, before {{ich}}.

lessons.title: Ask politely, without a straight question
lessons.summary: Ask strangers politely (“Do you know where the station is?”) and say what you don't know: “I don't know if he's coming.”
lessons.topic: Questions inside a sentence: {{Wissen Sie, wo…?}}, {{Können Sie mir sagen, wann…?}}; {{ob}} “whether, if” (verb last)

goal.t: Entschuldigung, wissen Sie, wo der Bahnhof ist?
goal.tr: Excuse me, do you know where the station is?

dialog.t: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir sagen, wann der nächste Zug nach Köln fährt?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, can you tell me when the next train to Cologne leaves?

dialog.t: Um vierzehn Uhr zwanzig, von Gleis fünf.
dialog.tr: At 2:20 p.m., from platform five.

dialog.t: Danke. Und wissen Sie, ob er Verspätung hat?
dialog.tr: Thanks. And do you know if it's late?

dialog.t: Im Moment nicht. Aber ich weiß nicht, ob das so bleibt!
dialog.tr: Not at the moment. But I don't know if it'll stay that way!

blocks.p: **A question inside a sentence.** A straight question can sound abrupt to a stranger: {{Wo ist der Bahnhof?}} So Germans often wrap it: {{Wissen Sie, wo der Bahnhof ist?}} “Do you know where the station is?” The wrapped question works like a {{weil}} or {{dass}} clause: the question word starts it, and its verb goes to the end.

table: {{Können Sie mir sagen, wann der Zug fährt?}}

blocks.p: **ob for yes/no questions.** A yes/no question has no question word, so inside a sentence it gets {{ob}} “whether, if”: {{Kommt er?}} → {{Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt.}} “I don't know if he's coming.” Careful: this “if” is {{ob}}, not {{wenn}}, which is for conditions.
**Useful openers:** {{Wissen Sie, …?}} “Do you know…?”, {{Können Sie mir sagen, …?}} “Can you tell me…?”, {{Ich weiß nicht, …}} “I don't know…”, {{Ich frage mich, …}} “I wonder…”.

ex.t: Können Sie mir sagen, wie spät es ist?
ex.tr: Can you tell me what time it is?

ex.t: Weißt du, wann der Film anfängt?
ex.tr: Do you know when the movie starts?
ex.note: a separable verb joins up at the end: {{anfängt}}

ex.t: Ich weiß nicht, wo meine Brille ist.
ex.tr: I don't know where my glasses are.

ex.t: Wissen Sie, ob hier ein Bus zum Flughafen fährt?
ex.tr: Do you know if there's a bus to the airport from here?

ex.t: Ich frage mich, warum er nicht anruft.
ex.tr: I wonder why he isn't calling.

ex.t: Kannst du mir sagen, was das heißt?
ex.tr: Can you tell me what that means?

blocks.tip: Being a little more polite with strangers is one of the quickest ways to sound good in German, and these openers do most of the work.

lessons.title: Talk about plans and the future
lessons.summary: Say what you're going to do (“Tomorrow I'm going to Hamburg”), and make predictions and promises: “Everything will be fine.”
lessons.topic: The present with a time word for plans; {{werden}} + infinitive for predictions, promises and resolutions

goal.t: Morgen fahre ich nach Hamburg. Das wird bestimmt toll!
goal.tr: Tomorrow I'm going to Hamburg. It's going to be great!

dialog.t: Was hast du nächstes Jahr vor?
dialog.tr: What are your plans for next year?

dialog.t: Im Januar fange ich einen neuen Job an.
dialog.tr: In January I'm starting a new job.

dialog.t: Toll! Und hast du gute Vorsätze?
dialog.tr: Great! And do you have any New Year's resolutions?

dialog.t: Ja. Ich werde mehr Sport machen und weniger arbeiten!
dialog.tr: Yes. I'm going to exercise more and work less!

dialog.t: Das sagst du jedes Jahr!
dialog.tr: You say that every year!

dialog.t: Ja, aber diesmal werde ich es wirklich machen. Versprochen!
dialog.tr: Yes, but this time I'll really do it. Promise!

blocks.p: **The present does most of the work.** For plans and arrangements, German usually uses the present with a time word: {{Morgen fahre ich nach Hamburg.}} “Tomorrow I'm going to Hamburg.”, {{Am Freitag haben wir ein Meeting.}} “We have a meeting on Friday.” The time word shows it's the future.

**werden + infinitive.** German also has a future tense: {{werden}} in second place and an infinitive at the end (one more verb bracket). It's for predictions ({{Es wird regnen.}} “It's going to rain.”), promises ({{Ich werde dich anrufen.}} “I'll call you.”), resolutions ({{Ich werde mehr Sport machen.}}), and for the future when there's no time word to make it clear.

**werden on its own** means “become, get”: {{Es wird dunkel.}} “It's getting dark.”, {{Sie wird Ärztin.}} “She's going to be a doctor.”, {{Das wird toll!}} “That's going to be great!” And remember: {{will}} means “want”. {{Ich werde kommen.}} “I will come.”, but {{Ich will kommen.}} “I want to come.”

ex.t: Nächste Woche besuche ich meine Eltern.
ex.tr: Next week I'm visiting my parents.
What are you doing on the weekend?
It's going to be cold tomorrow.
Don't worry, everything will be fine.

ex.t: Wann wirst du mit dem Studium fertig?

blocks.tip: {{Ich werde…}} as a promise is strong. For an everyday plan, the present sounds more natural: {{Ich rufe dich morgen an.}} “I'll call you tomorrow.”

The infinitive goes last.

lessons.title: Say what you're looking forward to
lessons.summary: Talk about your feelings and interests: “I'm looking forward to the weekend.” “I'm interested in art.”
lessons.topic: Verbs with {{sich}}: {{sich freuen auf}}, {{sich interessieren für}}, {{sich ärgern über}}, {{sich treffen}}

goal.t: Ich freue mich schon auf das Wochenende!
goal.tr: I'm really looking forward to the weekend!

blocks.means: a verb that comes with {{sich}} “oneself”, a pronoun pointing back to the subject: {{sich freuen}} “to be happy”, {{sich waschen}} “to wash (yourself)”.

blocks.p: **Verbs with sich.** Some German verbs need a little pronoun that points back to the subject, like English “myself”: {{Ich freue mich.}} “I'm happy”, word for word “I please myself”. Dictionaries list them with {{sich}}: {{sich freuen}}.
Only {{sich}} is new: for everyone else it's the object pronoun you already know ({{mich, dich, uns, euch}}). And polite {{Sie}} takes a small {{sich}}: {{Freuen Sie sich?}}

**Many come with a fixed preposition**, which you learn together with the verb: {{sich freuen auf}} “look forward to”, {{sich freuen über}} “be happy about”, {{sich interessieren für}} “be interested in”, {{sich ärgern über}} “be annoyed about”, {{sich erinnern an}} “remember”. The noun after them is in the accusative: {{Ich freue mich auf den Urlaub.}}

**Daily life** has lots of them too: {{sich duschen}} “shower”, {{sich anziehen}} “get dressed”, {{sich beeilen}} “hurry”, {{sich erholen}} “relax, recover”, {{sich setzen}} “sit down”, {{sich treffen}} “meet (up)”.

ex.t: Wir treffen uns um acht vor dem Kino.
ex.tr: We're meeting at eight in front of the movie theater.
Hurry up! The bus is coming!

ex.t: Er ärgert sich über das Wetter.

blocks.tip: {{Ich freue mich auf…}} (something coming) and {{Ich freue mich über…}} (something you've got) are two of the most useful phrases in German, in emails too: {{Ich freue mich auf Ihre Antwort.}} “I look forward to your reply.”

mistakes.right: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
mistakes.tr: I'm looking forward to the weekend.
mistakes.why: {{sich freuen}} needs its pronoun: {{mich}}.
Pointing back to {{er}}: {{sich}}. ({{ihn}} would be someone else!)
It's {{sich interessieren für}}: learn the preposition with the verb.
