lessons.title: Compare things and say what you prefer
lessons.summary: Compare things and people, and say what you like best: “The train is faster than the bus.” “I'd rather live in the country.”
lessons.topic: {{-er als}}, {{so … wie}}, {{am -sten}}; {{lieber}}, {{am liebsten}}; {{besser}}, {{am besten}}

goal.t: Berlin ist größer als München, aber München ist schöner.
goal.tr: Berlin is bigger than Munich, but Munich is prettier.

dialog.t: Welche Wohnung findest du am besten?
dialog.tr: Which apartment do you like best?

dialog.t: Die in Kreuzberg ist am größten, aber auch am teuersten.
dialog.tr: The one in Kreuzberg is the biggest, but also the most expensive.

dialog.t: Und die in Neukölln ist billiger als die in Mitte.
dialog.tr: And the one in Neukölln is cheaper than the one in Mitte.

dialog.t: Ja, aber die in Mitte ist so hell wie die in Kreuzberg!
dialog.tr: Yes, but the one in Mitte is as bright as the one in Kreuzberg!

dialog.t: Also, ich wohne lieber in Neukölln. Da ist es ruhiger.
dialog.tr: Well, I'd rather live in Neukölln. It's quieter there.

blocks.means: the form of an adjective that compares two things: bigger, more expensive.
the form of an adjective that says something is the most: biggest, most expensive.

blocks.p: **-er als: “-er than”.** German adds {{-er}} to every adjective, even long ones, and never uses “more”: {{schnell}} → {{schneller}}, {{teuer}} → {{teurer}}, {{interessant}} → {{interessanter}}. “Than” is {{als}}: {{Der Zug ist schneller als der Bus.}} Short words often get dots too: {{groß}} → {{größer}}, {{alt}} → {{älter}}, {{jung}} → {{jünger}}, {{warm}} → {{wärmer}}.

**am -sten: “the most”.** After a verb like {{sein}}, the superlative is {{am}} + adjective + {{-sten}}: {{am schnellsten}} “the fastest”, {{am teuersten}} “the most expensive”. Adjectives ending in {{-t}}, {{-d}}, {{-s}}, {{-ß}} or {{-z}} add {{-esten}} ({{am ältesten}}), except {{groß}}: {{am größten}}.
**so … wie: “as … as”.** {{Anna ist so alt wie Tom.}} “Anna is as old as Tom.”, {{nicht so … wie}} “not as … as”.

**What you prefer: lieber, am liebsten.** {{gern}} has its own forms: {{Ich trinke gern Kaffee.}} → {{Ich trinke lieber Tee.}} “I prefer tea.” → {{Am liebsten trinke ich Wasser.}} “Best of all, I like water.”

ex.t: Mein Bruder ist zwei Jahre älter als ich.
ex.tr: My brother is two years older than me.

ex.t: Heute ist es kälter als gestern.
Ich fahre lieber mit dem Zug.
Deutsch ist nicht so schwer wie Chinesisch.
ex.tr: German isn't as hard as Chinese.

blocks.tip: Never {{mehr}} with an adjective: not {{mehr schnell}} but {{schneller}}, not {{mehr interessant}} but {{interessanter}}. And “than me” is {{als ich}}.

mistakes.wrong: Der Zug ist schneller wie der Bus.
mistakes.right: Der Zug ist schneller als der Bus.
mistakes.tr: The train is faster than the bus.
mistakes.why: “Than” is {{als}}; {{wie}} belongs to {{so … wie}} “as … as”.
German adds {{-er}}, even to long adjectives.
{{gern}} → {{lieber}} → {{am liebsten}}.

lessons.title: Ask very politely
lessons.summary: Make requests that sound friendly and polite: “Could you help me?” “Would you sign here, please?” “That would be nice.”
lessons.topic: The Konjunktiv II for politeness: {{könnten}}, {{würden}}, {{hätten}}, {{wäre}}

goal.t: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
goal.tr: Could you help me, please?

dialog.t: Guten Abend. Ich hätte gern ein Zimmer für zwei Nächte.
dialog.tr: Good evening. I'd like a room for two nights.

dialog.t: Gern. Hätten Sie lieber ein Zimmer mit Balkon?
dialog.tr: Of course. Would you prefer a room with a balcony?

dialog.t: Ja, das wäre schön. Könnten Sie mich morgen um sieben wecken?
dialog.tr: Yes, that would be nice. Could you wake me at seven tomorrow?

dialog.t: Natürlich. Würden Sie hier bitte unterschreiben?
dialog.tr: Of course. Would you sign here, please?

dialog.t: Klar. Vielen Dank!
dialog.tr: Sure. Thanks very much!

blocks.means: a verb form for what is polite, wished for or imagined: {{ich hätte}} “I would have”, {{ich wäre}} “I would be”, {{ich würde}} “I would”.

blocks.p: **Softer verbs.** German makes a request polite with special forms of a few verbs, a bit like English “can” → “could”: {{Können Sie…?}} → {{Könnten Sie…?}} “Could you…?” You'll hear them all the time in shops, offices and hotels, and read them in every email.

**The forms** look like the past ({{konnte}}, {{hatte}}, {{war}}) with dots added: {{könnte}}, {{hätte}}, {{wäre}}. And {{würde}} “would” is the polite helper for every other verb, with the infinitive at the end: {{Würden Sie bitte hier unterschreiben?}}
**The politest opener of all:** {{Könnten Sie mir bitte sagen, …?}}: a Konjunktiv II plus a question inside a sentence. Start with it, and anyone will be glad to help.

ex.t: Könntest du mir das Salz geben?
ex.tr: Could you pass me the salt?
Would you speak more slowly, please?
Would Monday be OK for you?

ex.t: Könnten Sie mir bitte sagen, wo der Ausgang ist?
ex.tr: Could you please tell me where the exit is?

blocks.tip: {{könnten}} with dots means “could, would be able to”; {{konnten}} without dots is the past, “were able to”. Two little dots change the meaning!

mistakes.why: Without dots it's the past (“Were you able to help me?”). A polite request needs the dots: {{könnten}}.

mistakes.wrong: Würden Sie bitte schließen das Fenster?
mistakes.right: Würden Sie bitte das Fenster schließen?
mistakes.tr: Would you close the window, please?
mistakes.why: With {{würden}}, the infinitive goes last.

practice.q: Which one is a polite request?

lessons.title: Describe what you're looking for
lessons.summary: Describe things with adjectives in front of the noun: “I'm looking for a small apartment with a big balcony.” Adjective endings, part one.
lessons.topic: Adjective endings after {{ein}}, {{kein}}, {{mein}}: {{ein neuer Job}}, {{eine kleine Wohnung}}, {{einen guten Arzt}}

goal.t: Ich suche eine kleine Wohnung mit einem großen Balkon.
goal.tr: I'm looking for a small apartment with a big balcony.

dialog.t: Hallo, Sie rufen wegen der Wohnung an?
dialog.tr: Hello, you're calling about the apartment?

dialog.t: Ja. Ich suche eine helle Wohnung für meine Familie.
dialog.tr: Yes. I'm looking for a bright apartment for my family.

dialog.t: Die Wohnung hat drei Zimmer und eine neue Küche.
dialog.tr: The apartment has three rooms and a new kitchen.

dialog.t: Super. Gibt es auch einen kleinen Garten?
dialog.tr: Great. Is there a little yard too?

dialog.t: Nein, aber einen großen Balkon.
dialog.tr: No, but a big balcony.

dialog.t: Perfekt! Wir haben nämlich einen alten Hund.
dialog.tr: Perfect! We have an old dog, you see.

blocks.p: **In front of a noun, adjectives get endings.** After {{sein}}, an adjective has no ending: {{Die Wohnung ist klein.}} But in front of a noun it always has one: {{eine kleine Wohnung}}. The ending depends on the gender and the case.

**After ein, kein and mein.** These words don't always show the gender ({{ein}} could be masculine or neuter), so the adjective shows it instead: {{ein neuer Tisch}} (masculine, {{-er}} as in {{der}}), {{ein neues Auto}} (neuter, {{-es}} as in {{das}}), {{eine neue Lampe}} (feminine, {{-e}}).

**Only four endings.** {{-er}}: a masculine subject. {{-es}}: a neuter subject or object. {{-e}}: a feminine subject or object. {{-en}}: everything else (the masculine object, the whole dative, the plural). So when you're unsure in conversation, {{-en}} is the best bet.

ex.t: Wir wohnen in einem alten Haus.
ex.tr: We live in an old house.
Do you know a good dentist?

blocks.tip: With no article at all, the adjective shows the gender itself, with the ending of {{der/die/das}}: {{frisches Brot}} “fresh bread”, {{kalte Milch}} “cold milk”, {{guter Wein}} “good wine”, and {{liebe Grüße}} “best wishes” at the end of an email.

mistakes.why: In front of a noun, an adjective needs an ending: neuter, {{-es}}.
A masculine object: {{einen}} … {{-en}}.

mistakes.wrong: Wir wohnen in einem alter Haus.
mistakes.right: Wir wohnen in einem alten Haus.
mistakes.tr: We live in an old house.
mistakes.why: In the dative, always {{-en}}.

lessons.topic: Adjective endings after {{der}}, {{dieser}}, {{welcher}}: {{der blaue Pullover}}, {{mit dem roten Auto}}

goal.t: Ich nehme den blauen Pullover, nicht den schwarzen.
goal.tr: I'll take the blue sweater, not the black one.

dialog.t: Welcher Pullover gefällt Ihnen?
dialog.tr: Which sweater do you like?

dialog.t: Dieser blaue hier. Haben Sie ihn auch in L?
dialog.tr: This blue one here. Do you have it in a large too?

dialog.t: Ja. Und wie finden Sie die grüne Jacke?
dialog.tr: Yes. And what do you think of the green jacket?

dialog.t: Die grüne Jacke ist schön, aber die braune passt besser zu meinen neuen Schuhen.
dialog.tr: The green jacket is nice, but the brown one goes better with my new shoes.

dialog.t: Da haben Sie recht.
dialog.tr: You're right there.

blocks.p: **After der, the article already shows the gender**, so the adjective only needs a short ending: {{-e}} or {{-en}}. {{-e}} for the subject (all three genders) and for the feminine and neuter object; {{-en}} everywhere else.

**dieser and welcher** “this” and “which” take the endings of {{der/die/das}} ({{dieser, diese, dieses}}; {{welcher, welche, welches}}), and an adjective after them behaves exactly as after {{der}}: {{dieser blaue Pullover}}, {{Welche grüne Jacke?}}

**Leaving out the noun.** When it's clear what you mean, drop the noun and keep the article and adjective: {{den blauen}} “the blue one”, {{die grüne}} “the green one”. English needs “one”; German doesn't.

ex.t: Wie findest du das neue Restaurant?
ex.tr: What do you think of the new restaurant?

ex.t: Welchen Film möchtest du sehen? – Den neuen französischen.
ex.tr: Which movie do you want to see? – The new French one.

ex.t: Ich wohne in dem gelben Haus an der Ecke.
ex.tr: I live in the yellow house on the corner.

ex.t: Diese alten Fotos sind so schön!
ex.tr: These old photos are so beautiful!

ex.t: Der große Tisch passt nicht in die kleine Küche.
ex.tr: The big table doesn't fit in the small kitchen.

ex.t: Mit dem neuen Handy kann ich tolle Fotos machen.
ex.tr: With the new phone I can take great photos.

blocks.tip: Two systems, one logic: when the little word in front shows the gender clearly ({{der}}, {{dieser}}), the adjective relaxes ({{-e}}, {{-en}}); when it doesn't ({{ein}}, or no word at all), the adjective shows the gender itself ({{-er}}, {{-es}}).

mistakes.why: Masculine object after {{den}}: {{-en}}.
After {{der}}, the subject takes {{-e}}: {{der}} already shows it's masculine.

mistakes.right: Die Frau mit der roten Jacke ist meine Chefin.
mistakes.tr: The woman in the red jacket is my boss.
mistakes.why: In the dative, always {{-en}}.

lessons.topic: Relative clauses: {{der, die, das}} as “who, which, that”, with the verb at the end

blocks.means: a clause that describes a noun: the man **who lives next door**; the book **I'm reading**.

blocks.p: **A clause that describes a noun.** English uses “who”, “which” or “that”: “the man who lives next to me”. German uses {{der}}, {{die}} or {{das}} (the same words as “the”), after a comma, and the verb goes to the end: {{der Mann, der neben mir wohnt}}.

**der, die or das?** Two questions decide. Its gender and number come from the noun it describes: {{der Mann, der…}}, {{die Frau, die…}}, {{das Kind, das…}}, {{die Leute, die…}}. Its case comes from its job inside its own clause: subject, object (accusative), or dative.
Almost all of it is just {{der/die/das}} as you know them; only the dative plural is new ({{denen}}).

**German never leaves it out.** English can say “the book I'm reading”; German must say {{das Buch, das ich lese}}. And the commas around the relative clause are required. **With a preposition**, the preposition comes first: {{die Kollegin, von der ich erzählt habe}} “the colleague I told you about”, {{das Haus, in dem ich wohne}} “the house I live in”.

ex.t: Das Buch, das ich gerade lese, ist super.
ex.tr: The book I'm reading right now is great.

ex.t: Kennst du die Frau, die dort steht?
ex.tr: Do you know the woman standing over there?

ex.t: Wie heißt der Film, den wir gestern gesehen haben?
ex.tr: What's the name of the movie we saw yesterday?

ex.t: Das ist der Freund, mit dem ich nach Spanien fahre.
ex.tr: That's the friend I'm going to Spain with.

ex.t: Ich suche jemanden, der Deutsch und Englisch spricht.
ex.tr: I'm looking for someone who speaks German and English.

ex.t: Die Leute, denen das Haus gehört, wohnen in Hamburg.
ex.tr: The people who own the house live in Hamburg.

blocks.tip: In a relative clause, separable verbs join up at the end ({{der Zug, der um acht ankommt}}), and in the Perfekt {{haben}} or {{sein}} comes last ({{der Film, den wir gesehen haben}}): the same rules as after {{weil}}.

mistakes.wrong: Das ist der Mann, der wohnt neben mir.
mistakes.right: Das ist der Mann, der neben mir wohnt.

mistakes.wrong: Das Buch ich lese ist gut.
